term: "Perceptron"

## Simple explanation

A perceptron takes several inputs, gives each one a weight, adds a bias, and
uses the result to make an output. It is a basic building block for
understanding neural networks.

## Technical explanation

A common perceptron computes $y=\phi(\mathbf{w}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{x}+b)$,
where $\mathbf{x}$ is the input, $\mathbf{w}$ the weights, $b$ the bias,
and $\phi$ an activation function. The original threshold perceptron learns
a linear decision boundary and can represent only linearly separable
classification problems.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

The perceptron introduces weighted computation, activations, and learning
from examples. These ideas extend to multilayer networks, although modern
neural networks use many types of layers and optimization techniques beyond
the original perceptron learning rule.

## How it works

The unit calculates a weighted sum and passes it through an activation. In
the classic binary rule, the output is one when the sum crosses a threshold.
Training adjusts weights when the prediction is wrong; adding layers and
nonlinear activations allows networks to model more complex functions.

## Practical example

A single perceptron can learn the AND function from binary inputs, because
the positive examples can be separated from negative examples by a line.
One perceptron cannot learn XOR, whose examples are not linearly separable.

## Common misconceptions

- A single perceptron is not a deep neural network.
- The classic hard-threshold unit is not differentiable everywhere; modern
  networks usually use differentiable activations for gradient-based
  training.
